title: Casselman woman's death sparks bill to improve Ontario's 911 system
article: When Kathryn Missen called 911 on Labour Day 2014 in the middle of a severe asthma attack, she whispered faintly "I need a..." then gasped for breath as the operator tried to speak to her.
She died a short time later on the floor of her Casselman house, without ever getting the emergency medical care she needed.

A private member's bill, which was introduced Tuesday in the Ontario legislature, would help people like Missen whose so-called "no voice contact" to 911 call slipped through the cracks of an overburdened emergency response system.
It would be two days before police found her body, alerted by neighbours who were worried about the 54-year-old who lived alone.

The private member's bill, by NDP Nickel Belt MPP France Gélinas, stems from a coroner's inquest last fall into the deaths of Missen and three Sudbury area residents - Matthew Humeniuk, 33, Michael Kritz, 34, and Stephanie Bertrand, 25 - who died after their boat crashed into an island on Lake Wahnapitae in June 2013. A lone survivor spent more than an hour on the phone with a 911 dispatcher who could not figure out the crash location.
Gélinas's bill proposes an overhaul of the 911 system along the lines of the coroner's jury's 27 recommendations, including adding a 911 ombudsman to deal with complaints about the service.

"We, as a family, have always maintained that what happened to my sister Kathryn Missen was a failure of the system," said her sister, Brenda. " But while we were met with sympathy from officials at all levels, we were continually thwarted in our attempts to have an official review of the 911 system as a whole."

Among the bill's proposals are better training and oversight for 911 call centres, a common radio channel that would let paramedics, police and firefighters talk to each other, and technical upgrades that would allow dispatchers to quickly find the location of a cellphone caller. It would also extend 911 coverage completely across the province.

Of particular interest to the Missen family is the proposal to adopt technology in use in other jurisdictions that allows people who can't speak to communicate with the 911 dispatcher. Because Missen couldn't tell the dispatcher what was wrong, her call was given a low priority and eventually ignored altogether.
Missen's daughter, Harriet Clunie, and her three sisters were to be at Queen's Park Wednesday for a press conference with Gélinas. The bill is to be debated on May 2.

"My sister was a smart, witty, wise woman who had a generous heart and a strong sense of justice and fairness," Brenda Missen said. "The creation of the 9-1-1 Everywhere in Ontario Act will mean her death was not in vain."
